Source: AP and Reuters

Posted January 24, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: There is an old saying in the computer industry, garbage in, garbage out. The assumptions that went into this study assured its outcome. I really do not consider myself an expert on hemp, nonetheless, the flaws in this study seem obvious. This really is so dumb that only a prohibitionist wouldn’t be embarrassed by it, so I wonder if the results are being accurately reported or this is just the prohibitionist spin.

Notice that there is no mention of hemp’s uses in paper, building products or other areas. These are not speculative. They already exist. The ultimate size of these markets may be hard to predict, but ignoring them is inexcusable. Both the AP and Reuters seem to take the USDA study as definitive, although they do indicate that there is some disagreement.)

Study Finds Small Market for Hemp
By PHILIP BRASHER AP Farm Writer

WASHINGTON (AP) - Industrial hemp, the non-hallucinogenic cousin of marijuana that can be used in both clothing and food, will never have anything but a " small, thin market'' in the United States, a government study says.

(MarijuanaNews note: Marijuana is the non-hallucinogenic cousin of a mythical plant that is the subject of a lot of prohibitionist propaganda.)

All of the hemp fiber, yarn and fabric that the United States currently imports could be grown on less than 2,000 acres

of land, says the study by the Agriculture Department's Economic Research Service.

The study raises questions about efforts by farmers in a number of states to get the federal government to legalize production of industrial hemp.

(MarijuanaNews note: That is the real target of this study. It will be waived around by DEA agents at legislative hearings as proof that hemp is just a part of the plot to legalize all drugs for small children, premature babies and subatomic particles.)


See
DEA Fails to Intimidate County Council of Kauai on Hemp Cultivation in Hawaii

Nine states - Arkansas, California, Hawaii, Illinois, Minnesota, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota and Virginia - passed pro-hemp bills last year that provide for research, study or potential production of the crop, and the first U.S. test plots were planted in Hawaii last month.
See
Hawaii Gets DEA Permission To Grow Hemp Test Plot In Maximum Security,
Which Where They Want To Keep Hemp Users.
Alterna Issues Triumphant Press Release With Minimal Prohibitionist Propaganda

Some 35,000 acres were grown last year in Canada, which legalized hemp production in 1998.
(MarijuanaNews note: Canada grew 35,000 acres in just the first year of legal cultivation, but the current DEAland market would only require 2,000 acres? Canada has one tenth the population of DEAland, so it must export to other countries or use much more hemp per capita than DEAland. Of course, DEAland is the largest agricultural exporter in the world. In think that someone in the USDA is aware of that fact. )

The USDA study, which was released Friday, doesn't see much demand for any of hemp's uses:
-As a fiber, it's main competitor is linen, which is made from flax. There is little textile flax production in the United States, despite the lack of legal barriers, and that suggests there wouldn't be enough demand for hemp fiber to make it profitable, the study said.
(MarijuanaNews note: Presently, hemp is most like linen, but it could also compete with cotton in some markets. Most jeans are made of heavy cotton denim, and there are many other uses of coarse cotton that hemp might compete with. In its finer forms, hemp might also compete with other fabrics, including wool and synthetics. I have seen hemp fabrics that would never be mistaken for linen.)

-Hempseeds and flourare being added to nutrition bars, tortilla chips and other food items. USDA says that will probably remain a small use, comparable to the market for sesame and poppy seeds.
(MarijuanaNews note: Sesame and poppy seeds are put on the outside of foods for flavor, but the uses described here are for basic ingredients. Of course, they apparently missed the irony in the reference to poppy seeds. In these uses it could compete with oats and other grains. It might also compete with nuts such as pecans. The point is that even their own examples show the limits of their analysis.)

-As for hemp oil, it can't be used for frying, it has a short shelf life, and it hasn't been approved by the Food and Drug Administration as a salad oil.
(MarijuanaNews note: However, it is legal to put it on a salad. You may do so without any added risk of being shot in a no-knock raid. Even if it could be used for frying, that would be an extravagant waste of it for many years. Like soy bean oil, hemp seed oil can also be made into a variety of other products, and that is the really relevant comparison. Soy bean oil is a huge market.)

Hemp supporters say that new uses and markets for the crop will develop once it is clear to investors and companies that there will be a supply available.

" It's like soybeans 30 years ago,'' said Gale Glenn, a retired tobacco grower who is vice chairwoman of the North American Industrial Hemp Council. ``The markets will grow, but the markets aren't going to grow until they have the raw material.''
See
Tobacco Deal Forces Kentucky Farmers To Take Hemp Issue More Seriously

The Drug Enforcement Administration and the White House drug policy office say that legalizing hemp farming would make it more difficult to control marijuana production.
See
CBS Eye On America Let’s Drug Czar Barry McCaffrey Make a Fool Of Himself About Hemp Cultivation

January 21, 2000

Study douses high hopes for hemp as big U.S. crop

WASHINGTON, Jan 21 (Reuters) - Despite hemp's cachet as an up and coming textile, it probably never would be a financial bonanza for U.S. growers, a government study said on Friday, pouring cold water on some farm income hopes.

Industrial hemp, a cousin to mood-altering -- and illegal -- marijuana, has gained attention as an alternative to cotton for textiles and apparel as well as a possible cash crop for small farms.

The first test plots for industrial hemp were planted last month in Hawaii. Canada and Australia legalized hemp growing in 1998. Nine U.S. states, including Hawaii, passed legislation last year regarding research, study or production of the crop.

Agriculture Department economists concluded the market for industrial hemp " is and will likely remain a small, thin market.''

" Just a few farms'' could grow all the industrial hemp needed for domestic mills at present, they calculated. (MarijuanaNews note: Yes, but so what. That is like saying 20 years ago that just a few factories could make all the computers used.)

If hemp took away all of the linen market, it would require a comparatively small 250,000 acres (98,425 hectares) to grow it. That equals 40 percent of land now devoted to tobacco and 0.4 percent of land sown to wheat.
See
Tobacco Production Causes Global Environmental Damage
As DEAland Continues To Suppress Hemp Cultivation

Hemp enjoyed a surge of interest in tobacco states recently as farmers looked for substitutes for tobacco, a crop with far higher returns than cotton, corn or soybeans. Most growers have small farms so they need crops with large income per acre (hectare).

(MarijuanaNews note: Tobacco farmers have a long term problem, and hemp is presently one of the most promising possible substitutes, but the tobacco market has been artificially restricted for decades. Even hemp cannot replace government subsidies and licensed production as sources of income.)

The small volume of linen used each year " suggests that hemp, flax's close cousin in fiber uses and in production techniques, will be unable to sustain adequate profit margins for a large production sector to develop,'' the report said.

More than 1.5 million pounds (682,000 kg) of hemp fiber were imported last year. About 523,000 pounds (237,700 kg) of hemp fabric were imported in 1998 and hemp yarn imports peaked at 625,000 pounds (284,000 kg) in 1997. It would take about 2,000 acres (787 hectares) to grow that amount of hemp domestically, the economists said.

Canadian farms grew about 35,000 acres (13,800 hectares) of industrial hemp last year.

(MarijuanaNews note: The real problem with hemp as a savior for agriculture is simply that it will take decades to ramp up the processing and end use markets for hemp, as well as developing new products.
See
Canadians Find That Hemp Fields Are No Rose Garden.
Starting A New Crop Has Many Complications

That means that only a relatively small amount of acreage can be put in production each year. Consequently, hemp cannot save very many farmers who may be in trouble today. So why doesn’t the government just tell the truth, in stead of putting out such an embarrassingly dumb study?

The truth would be much more embarrassing, however, because it would make clear that the real reason that many farmers cannot be helped by hemp is that the government has suppressed it for decades during the greatest development of technology in agriculture and fabric development in history. Nonetheless, it is sad that the USDA is now just the agency in charge of sacrificing farmers to marijuana prohibition, just as HHS sacrifices health and human services to the same god. Obviously, the major news services are more than willing to sacrifice good journalism.)
